Real-valued random variables X and Y on Ω, inherited as elements/vectors of L²(Ω,Σ,P) for the full equality (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 1, anchor: “X : Ω → R”; PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.1) and Remark 1.1.1).

No independence, identical-distribution, zero-mean, nondegeneracy, or other exceptional-case assumption is imposed (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.2), whose displayed equality contains no such condition).
conclusions: cov(X,Y) = E[(X−E X)(Y−E Y)] = ⟨X−E X, Y−E Y⟩_{L²} (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.2)).

The centered product is formed in the displayed order: first X−E X, then Y−E Y; expectation applies to their whole product (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.2), together with PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 2).
definitions_and_conventions: E X denotes the Lebesgue integral of the real-valued function X:Ω→R with respect to the probability measure P (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 1).

The book drops expectation brackets and stipulates that nonlinear functions bind before expectation; hence E(X−E X)(Y−E Y) is E[((X−E X)(Y−E Y))] (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 2; PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.2)).
L²=L²(Ω,Σ,P) consists of random variables X with finite norm ∥X∥L²=(E|X|²)^{1/2} (PDF pages 1–2; printed pages 5–6, anchors: definition of Lp and Equation (1.1)).
For U,V∈L², ⟨U,V⟩_{L²}=E[UV]; in Equation (1.2), U=X−E X and V=Y−E Y (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equations (1.1)–(1.2)).
Within the selected passage, cov(X,Y) is expressed as the expectation of the product of the centered variables, equivalently their L² inner product (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.2)).

The source speaks literally of random variables as functions X:Ω→R and of Lp as consisting of such random variables; it does not explicitly state whether Lp elements are functions or equivalence classes modulo almost-sure equality (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 1 and the definition of Lp; PDF page 2; printed page 6, Hilbert-space paragraph).
implicit_context: All expectations, norms, covariance, and inner products use the same fixed probability measure P on (Ω,Σ,P) (PDF pages 1–2; printed pages 5–6, anchors: fixed probability space and Equations (1.1)–(1.2)).

Square-integrability of X and Y is inherited context: Equation (1.2) follows the definition of the L² Hilbert structure, and Remark 1.1.1 treats its variables as vectors in L² (PDF page 2; printed page 6).

Because P is a probability measure, X,Y∈L² implies finite means and integrability of the centered product; this well-definedness is a mathematical consequence of the cited probability/L² context, not a separately printed hypothesis of Equation (1.2).

No explicit quotient-by-almost-sure-equality convention occurs in the needed source context; adopting the standard quotient interpretation of Hilbert-space L² is therefore an interpretive convention rather than an explicit source statement (PDF pages 1–2; printed pages 5–6).

details: The domain is one fixed probability space (Ω,Σ,P), and the random variables are real-valued (PDF page 1; printed page 5, fixed-probability-space sentence and footnote 1).
E is integration with respect to P (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 1).
The bracket-dropping convention gives expectation scope over the complete centered product in Equation (1.2) (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 2; PDF page 2; printed page 6).
Each variable is centered by subtracting its own expectation: X−E X and Y−E Y (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.2)).
The displayed product orders the X-centered factor before the Y-centered factor (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.2)).
The inner product is ⟨U,V⟩L²=E[UV], so the last equality in (1.2) identifies covariance with the inner product of the centered variables (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equations (1.1)–(1.2)).
X,Y∈L² is inherited from the enclosing Hilbert-space discussion and Remark 1.1.1, not explicitly repeated in the sentence introducing Equation (1.2) (PDF page 2; printed page 6).

The text presents random variables as functions and never explicitly identifies almost-surely equal functions, while calling L² a Hilbert space (PDF pages 1–2; printed pages 5–6); the representative/quotient convention is therefore under-specified in the source.

contract_plain_english: On a fixed probability space (Ω,Σ,P), for real-valued square-integrable random variables X and Y, covariance is the expectation of the product obtained by centering X and Y separately, and this is exactly the L² inner product of those centered variables: cov(X,Y)=E[(X−E X)(Y−E Y)]=⟨X−E X,Y−E Y⟩L² (PDF page 2; printed page 6, Equation (1.2)). Expectation is integration with respect to P, and the bracket-free notation applies it to the whole product (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnotes 1–2). The source treats X and Y as L² vectors contextually but does not explicitly specify whether L² uses function representatives or almost-sure equivalence classes.
